sections.b:
After Revelation's letter to the church at Philadelphia (Revelation 3:7-13), Ignatius of Antioch passed through the city under guard on his way to Rome and met its overseer (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 1:1). Lightfoot traces the road: from the Lycus valley his guards took the northern route 'through Philadelphia and Sardis ... to Smyrna'. Later, from Troas, Ignatius wrote back. He had found 'not division' but 'filtering' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 3:1), yet he warns against anyone who 'interprets Judaism' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:1), recalls people who would believe nothing they could not find 'in the archives' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2), and says some suspected him and dishonored his companions (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 7:2; 11:1). Lightfoot takes these to be one group of Judaizers; the letter does not say so.

Lightfoot compares the two letters: Revelation praises the church's constancy, while Ignatius's picture 'is less favourable', though 'the main body of the Church appears to have been sound'. Revelation promises 'an open door' (Revelation 3:8); Ignatius calls Christ 'the Father's door' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 9:1).

sections.b: Lightfoot: the foundation of the Lydian Philadelphia is 'distinctly ascribed' to Attalus II of Pergamum, 'Philadelphus' (159-138 BC), though he adds 'we may be tempted to suspect an error', since John the Lydian says Egyptians founded it, which would point to Ptolemy Philadelphus. It lies at the foot of the Tmolus mountains on the road from the Maeander to Smyrna; it was famous for its wines and plagued by earthquakes, and it was among the cities thrown down under Tiberius. Its many temples and festivals earned it the name 'Little Athens', he reports from John the Lydian. Lightfoot counts eleven Christians from Philadelphia who died with Polycarp at Smyrna (Martyrdom of Polycarp 19:1, 'the twelfth together with those from Philadelphia').
sections.refs: Revelation 3:7-13; Martyrdom of Polycarp 19:1; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 1:0

common: Revelation 3:7-13 and Ignatius's letter are both written to the church at Philadelphia; Lightfoot calls Revelation 'The earliest notice of Christianity in Philadelphia'.
uncommon: Lightfoot thought the 'synagogue of Satan' of Revelation 3:9 and the Judaizers of Ignatius's letter point to a strong Jewish presence in the city.

sections.b: Written from Troas to a church Ignatius had visited (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 1:1; 7:1; 11:2). He calls it to 'one thanksgiving', 'one altar' and 'one overseer' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 4:1), recalls how he cried out among them 'in a loud voice, the voice of God' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 7:1), and answers those who would believe nothing they could not find 'in the archives': 'to me Jesus Christ is the archives' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 4:1; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 7:1-2; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 11:2

sections.b: At Philadelphia some told Ignatius: 'Unless I find it in the archives, I do not believe it in the gospel.' He answered 'It is written', they replied 'That is the question', and he concluded, 'to me Jesus Christ is the archives' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2). Lake and Lightfoot take 'the archives' as the Old Testament: the opponents would accept no Christian teaching they could not prove from it. The verse shows an early dispute about interpreting Scripture, settled for Ignatius by Christ's cross and resurrection. Its punctuation is debated: the Plain English Translation follows Lightfoot's; Lake prefers the common reading, 'I do not believe in the gospel' (see the note there).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2; Luke 24:25-27; Acts 17:2-3

sections.b: 'Be eager to use one thanksgiving. For there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup for union with his blood. There is one altar, as there is one overseer' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 4:1). The words build on 1 Corinthians 10:16-17. Lightfoot: 'The "one flesh" here is the one eucharistic loaf betokening the union in the one body of Christ', and the 'altar' is the gathered church rather than the table. Pohle in the Catholic Encyclopedia counts the verse among the witnesses to the Real Presence.

Ignatius warns: 'if anyone interprets Judaism to you, do not listen to him. It is better to hear Christianity from a circumcised man than Judaism from an uncircumcised one' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:1). Lightfoot takes the teachers to be Gentile Christians who urged Jewish ways from the prophets and 'the archives' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2); Lake says it is disputed whether they belonged with the docetists. Ignatius answers by honoring the prophets and priests (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 5:2; 9:1) and setting Christ above them.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:1; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 9:1; Galatians 2:14

sections.b: Ignatius's warning against those who 'interpret Judaism' is about teachers inside the church, and it prefers a circumcised man who teaches Christ to an uncircumcised one who teaches Jewish practice (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:1). It judges by what is taught, not by birth, and the same letter honors Israel's prophets and priests (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 5:2; 9:1). Read apart from that setting, his set phrase 'Judaism' against 'Christianity' was later used to set the two peoples against each other.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:1; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 5:2; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 9:1

sections.b: Ignatius says that while he was at Philadelphia he cried out 'in a loud voice, the voice of God: "Pay attention to the overseer"', and that it was 'the Spirit' preaching, not a human informant (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 7:1-2). The same letter loves 'the prophets', whom Lightfoot takes as Israel's and Lake as Christian prophets (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 5:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 7:1-2; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 5:2; 1 Corinthians 14:24-25

sections.b: 'The priests are good too, but better is the high priest, who has been entrusted with the most holy place' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 9:1). Lightfoot: the contrast is 'between the Levitical priesthood, and the great High-priest of the Gospel', after Hebrews; the long recension rewrote the line to speak of the Christian ministry.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 9:1; Hebrews 7:26-28; Hebrews 9:7

sections.b: Ignatius pictures the teachers as wolves 'that seem trustworthy' preying on 'God's runners' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 2:2) and as 'evil weeds' that are 'not the Father's planting' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 3:1, after Matthew 15:13). Yet the door stays open: 'all who repent and come to the unity of the church will belong to God too' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 3:2; 8:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 2:2; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 3:1-3; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:1; Matthew 15:13; Acts 20:29

sections.b: Ignatius greets the church 'above all if they are one with the overseer and with the elders and deacons who are with him' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 1:0), and says the overseer did not gain his ministry 'from himself or through human beings' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 1:1). Lightfoot reads 1:0 as human appointment confirmed by Christ's Spirit. The elders form 'the council of the overseer' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 1:0-1; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:1; Galatians 1:1

sections.b: Ignatius takes up 'I am the door' (John 10:9): Christ 'himself is the Father's door, and through it Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the prophets and apostles and the church come in' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 9:1).

From Troas Ignatius tells the Philadelphians that the church in Antioch of Syria is at peace and asks them to 'elect a deacon to be an envoy of God there'; nearer churches have sent overseers, elders and deacons (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 10:1-2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 10:1-2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2
